title: Two Random Choices Beat One Careful One: The Load Balancer Mental Model Nobody Teaches
description:
The problem

Picture a fleet of 100 identical workers behind a load balancer. You send requests uniformly at random — each request goes to a random worker, independent of the others. It sounds fair. It isn't.

If you send 100 requests to 100 workers this way, the most loaded worker doesn't get 1 request. On average, it gets around log(100) / log(log(100)) — roughly 4 to 5 requests — while plenty of workers sit idle. Send 10,000 requests to 10,000 workers and the busiest one gets over 9, not ~1. This isn't a bug in your random number generator. It's math, and it's called the "balls into bins" problem.

Most engineers have felt the symptom — a "perfectly balanced" random or round-robin-ish LB that still produces one hot node, one node pegged at 90% CPU while its siblings idle at 20% — without ever learning the mechanism. So they reach for the wrong fix: bigger instances, more replicas, a mysterious "just restart it" ritual. None of that touches the actual cause.

Why it happens

Uniform random assignment doesn't spread load evenly — it clusters, the same way random points in a room form clumps and empty patches instead of a neat grid. The formal result: if you throw n balls into n bins independently and uniformly at random, the maximum bin load is, with high probability, Θ(log n / log log n).

That's not linear in n, but it's not constant either — it grows, slowly but unboundedly, as your fleet scales. The more workers you add expecting things to smooth out, the more that log(n) term keeps producing a stubborn outlier. This is exactly why "just add more instances" often makes the imbalance more visible in absolute terms even as it helps in relative terms — the tail keeps growing with the fleet.

What to do about it

The fix has a name — the power of two choices (Azar, Broder, Karlin, Upfal, 1994; popularized for systems by Michael Mitzenmacher) — and it's absurdly cheap for how much it buys you.

Instead of picking one random worker, pick two random workers and send the request to whichever currently has less load. That's the entire algorithm. The result: the maximum load drops from Θ(log n / log log n) to Θ(log log n / log log log n) — an exponential improvement in the exponent. At n = 10,000, that's the difference between a worst node carrying ~9x the average and one carrying ~2-3x.

You've probably already used this without naming it:

  • Envoy's P2C (power-of-two-choices) load balancer is a built-in policy, not something you write yourself.
  • HAProxy's leastconn and AWS ALB's least-outstanding-requests algorithm are cousins of the same idea — they just skip the "pick two" sampling step and check global state directly, which works at small scale but gets expensive to coordinate globally at large scale (hence P2C's popularity: it needs no central coordinator).
  • Consistent hashing ring hot spots — the classic complaint that one shard runs hot even with a "good" hash function — are the same balls-into-bins effect. The standard mitigation, virtual nodes (100-200 vnodes per physical node), works by turning one ball into many smaller, independently-placed balls, which flattens the same log(n) tail.

The one gotcha that bites people who implement this from scratch: power of two choices needs reasonably fresh load signal. If your "current load" metric is stale — cached for 30 seconds, propagated through a slow gossip protocol — every requester samples the same stale "least loaded" node and stampedes it. You've now built a synchronized herd instead of a load balancer. The fix is either querying live local queue depth at decision time (what Envoy does) or adding jitter/randomization to which two nodes get sampled, so staleness doesn't correlate across requesters.

Key takeaways

  • Uniform random load balancing is not fair load balancing — balls-into-bins guarantees a growing max-load outlier as your fleet scales, Θ(log n / log log n).
  • Sampling two random candidates and picking the lesser-loaded one collapses that outlier to Θ(log log n / log log log n) — two lookups instead of one, no central coordinator required.
  • This is already built into Envoy, and it's the theoretical justification behind leastconn-style balancers you've probably deployed without reading the paper behind them.
  • The failure mode of power-of-two-choices itself is stale load data causing correlated stampedes — check freshness before you trust the "least loaded" signal.

title: Catch Bad Validation Tags at Compile Time with checkerlint
description:
Struct tags are just strings — a typo'd checker name, a wrong-typed field, or a renamed cross-field target all compile fine and fail silently at runtime. checkerlint catches all three before you ship.

Struct tags are string literals. The Go compiler checks that your struct compiles — it has no idea what checkers:"eq-field:Passwrd" means, so a typo in a field name, a checker applied to a field of the wrong type, or a renamed field that a cross-field rule still points at all compile fine. They fail later, at runtime, sometimes silently, sometimes as a panic in the middle of handling a request.

type Registration struct {
    Password        string `checkers:"trim required"`
    ConfirmPassword string `checkers:"required eq-field:Passwrd"` // typo: no such field
    Age             int    `checkers:"email"`                     // email is string-only
}

Nothing here trips go build, go vet, or a normal linter — they all treat checkers:"..." as an opaque string. The first bug only surfaces the moment someone submits a registration form and eq-field can't find a field called Passwrd. The second is worse: email assumes a string under the hood, so calling it on an int field panics at validation time instead of returning a normal error.

checkerlint is a go/analysis-based static analyzer, shipped as its own module in the Checker repo, that reads these tags at build/lint time and catches exactly this class of bug before it ships:

./registration.go:3:2: checkerlint: eq-field references field "Passwrd", which doesn't exist on this struct
./registration.go:4:2: checkerlint: email requires a string, but the field's type is int

What it actually checks

Three things, all specific to how checkers/validate tags can go wrong:

  1. Unknown checker names. Every token in the tag has to be a registered checker, normalizer, field-relative checker, omitempty, or a name your own code registered via RegisterMaker/RegisterFieldMaker with a string literal. Typo requird instead of required and checkerlint flags it — nothing else in your toolchain will.
  2. Type compatibility. A well-scoped set of built-ins panic at runtime on the wrong kind — string-only checkers (email, trim, url, and friends) and numeric-only ones (gt, gte, lt, lte). checkerlint checks the tagged field's actual type against what the checker expects, including through one level of pointer indirection and through a slice/array/map's element type for item-level tokens.
  3. Cross-field targets. eq-field, after-field, before-field, required-if, and required-unless all name a sibling field by string. checkerlint confirms that field actually exists on the struct — including, on a best-effort basis, embedded/anonymous fields — so a rename doesn't silently leave a dangling reference.

It knows the built-in vocabulary from whichever version of github.com/cinar/checker/v2 your code is built against, so it stays in sync automatically as new checkers ship. It can't see a checker registered only at runtime in a separate package, or one whose name is built from a non-literal expression — both are edge cases outside what static analysis can reach.

Running it

Install the standalone binary:

go install github.com/cinar/checker/v2/checkerlint/cmd/checkerlint@latest

Run it like go vet — same flags, same package patterns:

checkerlint ./...

Or plug it into go vet directly as a vet tool:

go vet -vettool=$(which checkerlint) ./...

Wiring it into golangci-lint

If your CI already runs golangci-lint, add checkerlint as a module plugin (golangci-lint v2's plugin system) instead of a separate step:

# .golangci.yml
version: "2"
linters:
  settings:
    custom:
      checkerlint:
        type: module
        path: github.com/cinar/checker/v2/checkerlint
        settings: {}

Module-plugin build steps have shifted across golangci-lint releases, so check its module-plugin docs for the exact setup your version expects — the .golangci.yml shape above is the stable part.

Why this matters more than it sounds like

Every struct-tag-driven validation library has this exact blind spot — go-playground/validator, ozzo-validation, all of them. The tags are strings; the compiler can't see inside them. Most teams find out about a typo'd checker name or a stale cross-field reference the way you'd expect: a bug report, or a support ticket about a validation rule that "just doesn't work," usually for a code path that isn't covered by a test with that exact malformed input.

checkerlint moves that failure from "someone hits it in production" to "the linter fails your PR." That's a category of bug — silently wrong or panicking struct tags — that the rest of the Go toolchain has no way to see, closed at the point where it's cheapest to fix.

Try it 

go install github.com/cinar/checker/v2/checkerlint/cmd/checkerlint@latest
checkerlint ./...

Full details, including exactly which checkers are type-checked, are in the checkerlint README. It's a separate, independently versioned module — adding it to your CI doesn't add a single dependency to the core checker library your code actually imports.

title: 15 Web & Cloud Terms Every Non-Technical Founder Should Actually Understand
description:
Ever nod along in a meeting when someone says "we need to sort out the CDN before we scale the backend," and quietly hope nobody asks you to explain what that means?

You're not alone.

I'm going to explain 15 terms that come up constantly when a business builds or scales a website, app, or SaaS product — without the academic definitions nobody asked for. If you already know these, this isn't for you. If you don't, and you're tired of pretending you do in client calls, keep reading.

To make it stick, let's follow a small business owner through her first year of going digital. Her name is Nadia, and she runs a bakery called Nadia's Sourdough. She's excellent at bread. She is not, by her own admission, excellent at "the internet stuff."

Let's go.

1. Domain Name

What is it?

The address people type to find your website. nadiassourdough.com, not the string of numbers the internet actually uses behind the scenes.

Nadia bought her domain in about four minutes and then spent three days trying to decide between .com and .co.nz. Completely normal. Nobody warns you that the domain name decision takes longer than naming your firstborn.

2. Hosting

What is it?

The computer (usually a server sitting in a data centre somewhere) that actually stores your website's files and serves them to visitors. Your domain name is the address; hosting is the building the address points to.

Nadia initially assumed "hosting" meant something to do with catering. It does not. Though to be fair, bad hosting can leave your site as unavailable as a bakery that's run out of bread.

3. SSL Certificate

What is it?

The thing that turns http:// into https:// and gives visitors that little padlock icon. It encrypts data between your site and your visitor, so nobody can snoop on it mid-transit.

Nadia didn't care about this until her web developer mentioned browsers actively warn visitors away from sites without one. Suddenly she cared a great deal.

4. CMS (Content Management System)

What is it?

Software that lets you edit your own website — add a blog post, change a price, swap a photo — without touching code. WordPress is the most common one.

Nadia can now update her menu herself instead of emailing her developer every time she adds a new sourdough flavour. This single feature has probably saved more client relationships than any other item on this list.

5. UI vs UX

What is it?

UI (User Interface) is what something looks like — buttons, colours, layout. UX (User Experience) is how it feels to use — is it confusing, is it fast, does the checkout button hide where nobody can find it.

You can have gorgeous UI and terrible UX. Nadia's first site had a beautiful hero image and an "Order Now" button that, when clicked, did absolutely nothing. Great UI. Catastrophic UX.

6. Front-End vs Back-End

What is it?

Front-end is everything the visitor sees and clicks on. Back-end is everything happening on the server that they don't see — processing the order, checking stock, charging the card.

Nadia's front-end shows a nice photo of a cinnamon loaf. Her back-end quietly checks whether she actually has any cinnamon loaves left before letting someone pay for one. When that check doesn't exist, you get the timeless business classic: selling bread you don't have.

7. API

What is it?

A defined way for two pieces of software to talk to each other. Instead of Nadia's ordering system rebuilding a payment processor from scratch, it just asks Stripe's API to "please charge this card," and Stripe handles the scary part.

APIs are why nobody has to reinvent GPS, weather data, or credit card processing every time they build something new. Everyone just asks the specialist.

8. Full-Stack Development

What is it?

Working across both the front-end and back-end of a project, rather than specialising in just one.

When Nadia's ordering site needed a nicer menu page and a fix for the stock-checking bug in the same week, a full-stack developer handled both without a handoff meeting. Efficient, if slightly less glamorous-sounding than "I specialise exclusively in buttons."

9. Database

What is it?

Where your actual data lives — customer orders, stock levels, account details — structured so it can be searched and updated quickly.

Nadia's database currently contains 40 customer names, 6 bread types, and one entry for "Gary — allergic to literally everything, call before delivering." Small, but sacred.

10. Cloud Hosting

What is it?

Instead of your site living on one physical server that falls over the moment it gets popular, cloud hosting spreads the load across many machines that can scale up automatically when traffic spikes.

Nadia's site got mentioned by a local food blogger and traffic tripled overnight. Because she was on cloud hosting, the site scaled with it. Her cousin's site, hosted on a single ageing server under someone's desk, did not survive its own viral moment quite so gracefully.

11. CDN (Content Delivery Network)

What is it?

A network of servers around the world that cache copies of your site so it loads fast no matter where the visitor is, instead of every request travelling back to one server on the other side of the planet.

Nadia's cousin in London complained the site "felt slow." Once a CDN was added, it stopped feeling like her photos of sourdough were travelling by actual ship.

12. SaaS (Software as a Service)

What is it?

Software you access online and pay for on subscription, rather than installing and owning outright. Think an ongoing rental, not a one-time purchase.

Nadia doesn't run a SaaS herself, but she uses about six of them daily without noticing: her booking calendar, her accounting software, her email tool. Modern small business, held together entirely by other people's monthly subscriptions.

13. Multi-Tenancy

What is it?

The architecture that lets one SaaS platform serve many different customers ("tenants") from the same underlying system, while keeping each customer's data completely separate.

The booking calendar Nadia uses serves thousands of businesses from one platform. She sees her own bookings. She does not see her competitor's, or anyone else's — that separation is the entire point, and it's much harder to build properly than it sounds.

14. CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment)

What is it?

An automated pipeline that tests and ships code changes without a human manually copying files onto a server and hoping for the best.

When Nadia's developer fixed the stock-checking bug, CI/CD tested the fix automatically and deployed it within minutes. In a world without CI/CD, that fix waits for someone to remember to upload it manually, usually right before they go on holiday.

15. Bounce Rate

What is it?

The percentage of visitors who land on your site and leave without doing anything else — no clicks, no scrolling, nothing.

Nadia's bounce rate dropped noticeably after fixing the broken "Order Now" button from item #5. Turns out people leave quickly when the thing they came to do doesn't work. Genuinely shocking research findings.

That's 15. There's a longer list I could've kept going with — hosting uptime, load balancers, DNS propagation, the eternal mystery of why cache clearing fixes everything — but fifteen is already a lot to absorb before lunch.

If you're a founder who's been quietly Googling half these terms during client calls: you're further ahead than you think, and now you at least have the vocabulary to ask better questions of whoever's building your site.

What term took you the longest to actually understand? Mine was CDN — I spent an embarrassingly long time assuming it was just a fancier word for hosting.

title: Open-source tool: Practical experience in converting large quantities of SQL code syntax : 'PIVOT' function rewrite (Case 1)
description:
Background : In migration projects involving different databases, incompatibility of SQL syntax is often encountered.

Question : If there is a large amount of code that needs to be rewritten, manual processing would be time-consuming and prone to errors. Is it possible to achieve automatic conversion of code syntax in large quantities through tools?

Solution : The open-source tool ZGLanguage can be utilized to perform automated conversion of SQL code in large batches.

For example：

Suppose SQL PIVOT function is as follows :

SELECT *
FROM (select country,state,yr,qtr,sales,cogs from table111)
PIVOT
(
    SUM(sales) AS ss1,
    SUM(cogs)  AS sc 
    FOR qtr IN 
    (
        'Q1' AS Quarter1,
        'Q2' AS Quarter2,
        'Q3' AS Quarter3,
        'Q4' AS Quarter4
    )
) tmp
;

Using the ZGLanguage conversion rule, execute the conversion to obtain the result :

SELECT *
FROM 
(
  select ###,###,###
         SUM (case when qtr='Q1' then sales else null end) AS Quarter1_ss1,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q2' then sales else null end) AS Quarter2_ss1,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q3' then sales else null end) AS Quarter3_ss1,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q4' then sales else null end) AS Quarter4_ss1,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q1' then cogs else null end) AS Quarter1_sc,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q2' then cogs else null end) AS Quarter2_sc,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q3' then cogs else null end) AS Quarter3_sc,
         SUM (case when qtr='Q4' then cogs else null end) AS Quarter4_sc
  from (select country,state,yr,qtr,sales,cogs from table111) 
 where qtr IN('Q1','Q2','Q3','Q4')
 group by ###,###,###
) tmp
;

Detailed explanation of conversion rules：

The conversion rules of PIVOT function mentioned above are quite complex, it cannot be converted all at once, needs to be completed through 3 conversions.

ZGLanguage -e PIVOT_UNPIVOT_SQL_REPLACE.syn -r pivot_unpivot.code -o 1_mid_result.zgl
ZGLanguage -e PIVOT_UNPIVOT_SQL_REPLACE.syn -r 1_mid_result.zgl -o 2_mid_result.zgl
ZGLanguage -e PIVOT_UNPIVOT_SQL_REPLACE.syn -r 2_mid_result.zgl -o result.zgl

The first conversion, trigger the rule 'FROM_PIVOT_1_1' to convert the source code, complete the one-to-one mapping between the value "qtr" and the enumeration values "Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4", and result were obtained as follows:

(
    SUM(sales ) AS ss1 ,
    SUM(cogs) AS sc
    FOR qtr IN
    (  
    qtr = 'Q1' AS Quarter1 ,  
    qtr = 'Q2' AS Quarter2 ,  
    qtr = 'Q3' AS Quarter3 ,  
    qtr = 'Q4' AS Quarter4
    )
) tmp
;

The 2nd conversion, trigger the rule 'FROM_PIVOT_1_2' to convert the above conversion result again.

To complete :
(A) Cartesian product of "SUM" columns and "qtr" columns
(B) Convert "FOR" structure to "where" structure

And result were obtained as follows:

SELECT *
FROM (select country,state,yr,qtr,sales,cogs from table111) PIVOT
(
    SUM(sales) AS ss1   qtr = 'Q1' AS Quarter1 ,
    SUM(sales) AS ss1   qtr = 'Q2' AS Quarter2 ,
    SUM(sales) AS ss1   qtr = 'Q3' AS Quarter3 ,
    SUM(sales) AS ss1   qtr = 'Q4' AS Quarter4 ,

    SUM(cogs) AS sc     qtr = 'Q1' AS Quarter1 ,
    SUM(cogs) AS sc     qtr = 'Q2' AS Quarter2 ,
    SUM(cogs) AS sc     qtr = 'Q3' AS Quarter3 ,
    SUM(cogs) AS sc     qtr = 'Q4' AS Quarter4 

    where qtr IN
    (
        'Q1' ,
        'Q2' ,
        'Q3' ,
        'Q4'
    )
) tmp
;

The 3rd conversion, trigger the rule 'FROM_PIVOT_1_3' to convert the above conversion result again.

To complete :
(A) Perform operations such as adding, shifting, and merging on the field content starting with SUM to form a syntactically correct field code.
(B) Delete key word 'PIVOT', move the subquery above the 'where' statement.
(C) Newly added parts to be manually supplemented: select ###,###,###   group by ###,###,###

Obtain the finally result:

SELECT *
FROM 
(
  select ###,###,###
         SUM(case when qtr='Q1' then sales else null end) AS Quarter1_ss1,

 where qtr IN('Q1','Q2','Q3','Q4')

title: The Julius AI free plan: what the free credits actually get you
description:
If you are searching for the Julius AI free plan, you are almost certainly asking one question: can I actually get my work done without paying? Here is the line that settles it before any credit arithmetic: the free plan has no database connector at all. Its Free column lists Google Drive, OneDrive and Sharepoint; Snowflake, BigQuery and Postgres begin on Plus at $20/mo. So if the numbers you need to ask about live in a database, the size of the free credit grant never enters into it. If they live in files, the credits are then the whole question — and the honest answer on those, from Julius's own documentation, is that the free plan is not a plan you live on. It is a small allowance meant for an evaluation rather than for ongoing work. Whether it runs out permanently or refills at a low daily rate is one of the things Julius does not say consistently, which is the next section — but under either reading it is an allowance you finish, not one you work inside.

One thing to settle before you spend ten minutes here, because it disqualifies a lot of readers immediately. If the data you work on arrives as files — a spreadsheet a client emailed you — then Julius's free plan opens it and the Intellrise free tier cannot, at any tier below Pro. That is the single biggest difference between the two free plans and it is not close. This page is written for the case where the data you need to ask questions about sits in a database. If your work starts with a file on your laptop and you need it to stay free permanently, the honest answer is Julius. One fact before you decide, because it is the one most likely to change the answer: every new Intellrise account starts on 14 days of Pro with no card, and file upload is part of Pro. So a file is free to test here — what Julius does and we do not is keep it free after that.

How small, exactly, is the part nobody can tell you from the outside — including us. Julius's billing documentation described the Free grant as "100 (one-time)" credits that "don't renew" when we read it on 3 August 2026; by 28 August 2026 that same table said "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily credits" instead, and the figure of 100 survived only in the FAQ lower down the page; the pricing page's comparison table describes the Free column only as "Free daily credits" and gives no number anywhere. We quote all three below with the dates we read them. We are not going to pick one for you and present it as settled, because we cannot see your account — but every version agrees the allowance is small and that a live database is not part of it, and those two facts are usually what the decision turns on.

This guide covers what the free plan includes, the three limits that catch people out, where Julius's own pages disagree with each other, and where Julius's free plan is genuinely the better choice than ours. Every Julius figure below was read from a Julius-owned page — on 3, 13 and 28 August and again on 6 September 2026 — and each one carries the date we read it. If you want the full cost breakdown across all the paid tiers instead, read our Julius AI pricing guide.

If what you actually want is a plan you can work inside rather than an allowance you finish, that is a fortnight of ordinary work away from being settled either way.

Start free — 14 days of Pro, no card

First, the question that decides whether any of this applies to you: can we reach your database?

Intellrise connects from our servers, not from your browser, so your database has to accept a connection from the internet, and the account you give us has to be read-only. That second one stays your control, not ours — and when you connect we check whether you used one: Intellrise asks your database what that account is allowed to do and puts the answer on the connection screen. It reports, it never blocks, and it says so plainly when it cannot tell. On our side we also refuse the statements we send. Three sources skip that question entirely: BigQuery, Google Sheets and uploaded CSV or Excel files need no inbound rule at all, because there is no port to open. If you do open one, the page below has the checklist, the copy-paste GRANT statements for four databases, the two outbound ranges we connect from, and the TLS position per database type: Postgres always connects with sslmode=require and there is no setting to turn it off, while MySQL, SQL Server and Redshift follow whatever your server negotiates.

Can Intellrise connect to my database?

The other prerequisite is an AI provider key of your own, on every plan including the trial. A Google Gemini key is free and takes about a minute:

How do I get a free AI key?

The short answer

  • The free plan costs $0, and the size of the grant depends on which Julius page you read. Its billing FAQ says free users "receive a one-time grant of 100 credits when they sign up; these credits don't renew"; the credits table on that same page said "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily credits" when we re-read it on 13 August 2026, and still said it on 28 August 2026. Both are quoted in full further down.
  • Credits do not roll over and cannot be topped up. Asked whether unused credits roll over, Julius answers "No. Unused credits expire at the end of your billing cycle and don't carry over." On buying more: "At the moment, purchasing additional credits or topping up your balance is not supported."
  • There is no free trial of the paid tiers. The words "trial", "free trial" and "credit card" do not appear anywhere on the Julius pricing page — we checked the rendered page and the underlying data payload. The free plan is the trial.
  • You cannot connect a database on Free. The pricing comparison table's Data connectors row lists "Google Drive, OneDrive, Sharepoint" for Free; Snowflake, BigQuery and Postgres appear only from Plus upward.
  • Four of the headline features are "Limited" on Free rather than included. Reading the pricing comparison table on 6 September 2026, the Free column says "Limited" for AI Presentation Maker, AI Image Generator, AI Video Generator and Build Websites with AI, while all four carry a tick in every paid column; Scheduled Runs is not offered on Free or Plus at all and starts at 3 on Pro. Julius does not publish what "Limited" amounts to, so it is one more thing you can only size by spending the grant.
  • Uploaded files are deleted after an hour of inactivity. Julius's file documentation is explicit: free-tier files are "retained for up to 1 hour of inactivity, after which all uploaded and AI-generated files are deleted". Paid users get 7 days.
  • Julius no longer counts messages at all. If you have read an older comparison quoting a monthly message cap for Julius, it is out of date — the docs now say "Instead of counting messages, Julius now measures usage in credits."

Where Julius's own pages disagree about the free plan

This is the part worth reading slowly, because it is the reason the free plan is hard to research. Julius maintains a marketing pricing page and a separate documentation site, and the table below puts the same five questions to both. When we first ran it on 3 August 2026, four of the five came back with two different answers. When we ran it again on 28 August 2026, two of those four had been reconciled, one had changed its numbers on us, and one was unchanged. We are not claiming either page is dishonest — docs and marketing pages drift apart at every company, including ours. But if you are deciding whether the free plan is enough for you, you should know which number you are trusting, and you should know how fast that answer moves.

Run the same audit on us, because it is the only reason to believe the rest of this page. Every Intellrise figure here comes from one place — our own pricing page and the product itself — and if you find two Intellrise pages disagreeing about a limit, that is a bug rather than a positioning decision, and telling us is enough to get it fixed.

Question julius.ai/pricing says Julius docs say
How many free credits? The Credits row for Free still reads "Free daily credits" with no number given anywhere on the page (28 August 2026) Two answers on one page (28 August 2026): the credits table now reads "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily credits" and the prose beneath it "The Free plan's 25 welcome bonus credits are a one-time grant and don't renew", while the FAQ further down still says free users "receive a one-time grant of 100 credits when they sign up". On 3 August that table row read "Free — 100 (one-time)"; it does not any more
Do they recur? "daily" implies a recurring allowance; "Daily refresh credits" is separately listed as a feature of the paid cards only They do not recur. "these credits don't renew"
How much memory? Nothing at all: RAM, GB and sandbox return zero matches across the whole page (28 August 2026). On 3 August the Free card and a System memory row read "2 GB of RAM"; that row has left the page Unchanged and now the only published figure: the Standard container is "8 GB" and is marked "All plans", with "Memory Boost" at "32 GB" on "Pro plan and higher" (julius.ai/docs/get-started/containers, 28 August 2026)
Which models on Free? No longer a disagreement, and we are saying so: on 28 August 2026 the Models row reads "Julius Lite models" for Free, "Julius models, GPT-5.6, Claude Sonnet 5" for Plus and "All models, including Claude Fable 5" from Pro up. On 3 August it showed Free as identical to Plus "Julius 1.2 Lite" is "All plans"; every other model listed is "Paid plans" or higher (28 August 2026). The two pages now agree — Julius fixed this one between our reads, and leaving the old accusation up would have been the easy thing to do
What is the metering unit? The word "message" still does not appear on the pricing page at all (0 matches, 28 August 2026) "Instead of counting messages, Julius now measures usage in credits"

The three limits that actually decide it

Credit counts are the headline, but in practice three other constraints determine whether the free plan can do your job.

  • No live data connection. The free plan reads files from Google Drive, OneDrive and Sharepoint. If your data lives in Postgres, MySQL, Snowflake or BigQuery, the free plan cannot reach it — that capability starts on Plus at $20/mo ($16/mo billed yearly). For anyone evaluating an AI analyst against a real warehouse, this is usually the deciding line rather than the credit count.
  • Files vanish after an hour idle. Because free-tier files are deleted after an hour of inactivity, the free plan does not support coming back to yesterday's analysis. It supports one sitting. That is a reasonable design for a trial and a poor one for recurring reporting.
  • The grant is small, and you cannot price it in advance. On the one-time reading there is no steady state at all; on the 25-a-day reading there is one, but it is a low daily ceiling rather than a budget you can save up, because credits do not roll over and cannot be topped up. Either way Julius does not publish a per-action credit price — its FAQ says directly that there is "no single answer" because cost depends on the message complexity and which tools are invoked — so you cannot convert the grant into a number of questions in advance. You find out by spending it. One wrinkle before you plan on buying your way out: the same billing page that says top-ups are not supported also carries a refund clause governing them, word for word — "Credits are non-refundable, whether you bought them as a top-up or received them through your subscription" (julius.ai/docs/billing/credits-overview, read 28 August 2026). The ordinary explanation is that refund policies are drafted to cover more than a product currently ships, and we are not going to call it anything worse than that. It does mean the page cannot tell you whether top-ups are coming back, so if your plan for running dry is "buy a few more", ask a human at Julius first. On the Intellrise free tier there is no grant to top up and nothing to run out of on our side: you attach your own AI provider key and pay that provider directly, so the ceiling is your own billing account rather than ours.

What $0 buys on the Intellrise side

The question that brought you here is whether free is enough to do your work, and you cannot answer it by reading one vendor's free column. So here is the same accounting for the Intellrise free tier, at the same level of detail, with the places it loses set out in the section after next rather than buried.

One note on how to read what follows, because the standard of proof is not the same on both sides. Every Julius figure on this page carries a URL and the date we read it, so you can check it yourself in a minute. The Intellrise claims below come from our own source code, which you cannot read — so treat them as things to verify rather than things to believe, and the fastest verification is a free account, which needs no card. Where a claim is about quality rather than mechanism we have said so and declined to make it.

One framing note before the list, because it decides which of these two is even relevant to you. Julius's free plan is built around files: you bring a spreadsheet, it reads it, and the meter counts what you spend. The Intellrise free tier is built around a connection: you point it at a database and supply your own AI key, and there is no meter. Neither shape is better in the abstract. They are better for different starting positions, and the starting position is where your data already lives.

  • One live database, and it can be a real one. The Intellrise free tier connects a single data source, and that source may be PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks or Redshift. Google Sheets is not counted against that one at all, and not as a second slot either: Intellrise excludes Sheets from the source quota entirely, with no separate cap on how many you connect. So a database plus however many Sheets you need is a free-tier configuration, and this is the one route by which mixed work — a client who gives you database access and two who email you spreadsheets — fits on $0, provided you are willing to land the spreadsheets in Sheets rather than upload the files. This is the line the two products draw in different places: Julius gates live database connectors at Plus, $20/mo, while on Intellrise the connection is the thing the free tier is for.
  • No credit meter, because there is nothing to meter. Intellrise does not resell model capacity — you supply your own provider key and pay that provider directly at their list price — so there is no allowance to run down, no top-up to buy and no counter in the corner of the screen. The usage endpoint in the product returns no limit at all rather than a number you are counting down from. Your ceiling is whatever your own AI account allows, which also means you pick the model and therefore the rate.
  • Every export format, on the free tier. CSV, Excel, PDF, PowerPoint and Word. The export route carries no plan check at all, so a free Intellrise account produces the same files a paying one does. For a lot of freelance and consulting work the deliverable is the whole job, and this is the limit that usually bites first elsewhere. Two caveats we would rather you read here than discover later: the document formats truncate long tables — PDF and PowerPoint show the first 30 rows and Word the first 100, with a line telling the reader how many were left off, while CSV and Excel carry everything — and the free tier has no share links and no email delivery, so getting the file to someone else is your job, not the product's.
  • AI report editing is on the free tier. Asking the assistant to rewrite a section of a generated report is guarded by a feature flag that is switched on for every tier, free included — it is the one piece of AI-assisted authoring in Intellrise that costs nothing beyond your own tokens.
  • No trial cliff, because the free tier is not a trial. An Intellrise free account does not expire, does not ask for a card and does not convert into anything at the end of a period. The fourteen-day Pro trial sits alongside it rather than replacing it: decline the trial and you are on the same Intellrise free tier you started on, with the same one live database and the same exports. That matters here because what you are really comparing is not two free plans but two evaluation paths — one where the allowance runs out and one where it does not. On Intellrise, outgrowing free is a decision you make, not a balance hitting zero.
  • Schema reading is not sampled down. Intellrise walks every table and every column the connection exposes rather than taking the first N, so a wide database does not get silently truncated on the way in. Being straight about what "exposes" covers, because until 23 August 2026 it covered less than that sentence implies: on PostgreSQL we read ordinary tables, partitioned parents, views and materialized views — but views and materialized views were invisible before that date, so if your reporting logic lived in a view, the model did not tell you it could not see it, it answered from the base tables instead. That is fixed and this is what it now reads. Two things it still does not read, both on Redshift: materialized views, and late-binding views, whose columns cannot be resolved until query time — we leave those out rather than hand the model a table name with no columns under it, because that is how you get invented column names. And all of this describes what the code does, not a published benchmark on somebody else's forty-table production schema. We have not run that benchmark in public, so do not take this as a promise about answer quality on a messy database — take it as the absence of an artificial cap.
  • Three dashboards, and reports are not rationed by the month. The free tier caps dashboards at three; it does not put a monthly ceiling on how many questions you ask or reports you generate, because there is no unit to ration.

What the free plan does include

It is a genuinely capable free tier for the file-first use case, and it is worth being precise about that rather than dismissive. On 28 August 2026 the Free card lists exactly three key features, quoted verbatim: "Create presentations, reports, websites, images, and video", "File storage formats" (tooltip: "Upload .csv, .xlsx, .sav"), and "Google Drive data connector". That is a different card from the one we quoted here on 3 August 2026, which listed "Access to Notebooks" and "2 GB of RAM": on 28 August 2026 the strings Notebooks, RAM and 2 GB return zero matches anywhere on that page, and Julius's own documentation now says, word for word, "Notebooks have been sunset" (julius.ai/docs/notebooks-sunset, read 28 August 2026). We are showing you both readings rather than quietly swapping one for the other, because the change is the point: the free tier you evaluated in July is not the free tier you would sign up for today, and Julius's pricing page carries no date of its own to warn you.

What has not changed is the limit on our side. Intellrise does not run arbitrary Python or R at any price — analysis here is read-only SQL — and the sunset of Julius's Notebooks does not narrow that gap, because the code execution underneath it is still there: Julius's own docs describe it "running code, querying data" as it works, and its visualization page names matplotlib, seaborn and plotly (read 28 August 2026). If your work needs a statistical library, that is a reason to use Julius rather than us. And .sav is SPSS, which matters if you are coming from academic or survey research; Intellrise does not read that format either.

The other shape of free: bring your own key

Intellrise's free tier is built on a different model, and the difference is worth understanding before you compare the two, because it changes what "free" means rather than just how much of it you get.

There is no credit meter on any Intellrise plan, free or paid. You supply your own AI provider key — Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, MiniMax or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — and you pay that provider directly for tokens at their list price. We do not resell model capacity, so there is nothing for us to ration. Your ceiling is whatever your own provider account allows, and you choose the model, which is the single biggest lever on cost.

The free tier connects one data source, and that source can be a live database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks or Redshift, plus Google Sheets which does not count against the one. That is the main practical difference from Julius's free plan — a live warehouse connection is the thing Julius gates and we do not.

On the free plan Julius Intellrise
Recurring allowance A small grant Julius's own pages size differently — "100 (one-time)" in one place, "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily" in another; no rollover, no top-up either way No credit meter. You pay your own AI provider directly for tokens
Live database connection Not included. Data connectors row lists Google Drive, OneDrive, Sharepoint; Snowflake, BigQuery and Postgres start on Plus One data source, which can be PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks or Redshift — plus Google Sheets, uncounted
File upload Included: .csv, .xlsx, .sav Not on Free. File upload (CSV/Excel) is listed on Pro
File retention Deleted after 1 hour of inactivity (paid: 7 days) Not applicable — the free tier reads a live connected source rather than storing uploads
Notebooks Sunset. Julius's docs say "Notebooks have been sunset" (read 28 August 2026) and the Free card no longer lists them; the code execution underneath continues Not offered on any plan
Models Docs mark only Julius 1.2 Lite as available on all plans; frontier models are marked paid Any model your own key can reach, including frontier models, on the free tier
Trial of the paid tier None offered; "trial" does not appear on the pricing page 14-day Pro trial, no card. The free tier remains after it lapses

Getting a key is the annoying step and we are not going to dress it up: you go to Google AI Studio, create a free Gemini key, and paste it in. It took us about a minute; it will feel like a detour. Everything after it is free to try, because a new account also starts on 14 days of Pro.

Start your 14-day Pro trial

14 days of Pro, no credit card. After it lapses the free tier stays free.

Where Julius's free plan is the better choice

We would rather you pick the right tool than pick ours, so here is the honest version. If any of these describe you, Julius's free plan will serve you better than the Intellrise one will, and you should take it.

  • Your data is a spreadsheet on your laptop. Julius's free plan accepts .csv, .xlsx and .sav uploads. The Intellrise free tier does not — file upload sits on Intellrise Pro, so a free Intellrise account cannot open your file at all.
  • You want to ask a question in the next five minutes. Julius runs on its own platform key, so you sign up and type. Every Intellrise plan is bring-your-own-key with no platform fallback, which means you must go and create a key with an AI provider before you can ask a single question. That is real friction and we are not going to pretend otherwise.
  • You want to run Python or R. The code execution did not leave with the notebooks, and the docs are explicit about it: julius.ai/docs/get-started/tools says "Julius writes Python or R and runs it in a secure cloud container", and its visualization page names matplotlib, seaborn and plotly (both read 28 August 2026). Intellrise runs read-only SQL and has no code execution at any price. One correction to an earlier version of this page: if it was specifically the cell-based notebook you wanted, neither tool has one for you now — julius.ai/docs/notebooks-sunset says "Notebooks have been sunset" (read 28 August 2026).
  • You work in SPSS. Julius reads .sav. Intellrise reads CSV and Excel.
  • You need it for one afternoon. A grant this size is a perfectly good fit for a single evaluation sitting, which is what it is designed for. The afternoon itself is covered on our side too — a new account's 14 days of Pro include file upload — so the honest difference is the step before it: you have to create an AI provider key here before you can ask anything, and Julius runs on its own.
  • Your data is a file, not a database. This is the whole ballgame. Julius Free reads .csv, .xlsx and .sav from Drive, OneDrive and SharePoint; the Intellrise free tier cannot accept an uploaded file on any plan below Pro. If your work starts with a spreadsheet somebody emailed you, Julius Free keeps doing it for nothing and our free tier never does — the 14 days of Pro that open your file first are the paid tier, not this one.

If the file is in your hand right now, Julius's free plan is the faster route today. If the data lives in a database, that is the case worth testing here.

Connect a database, free for 14 days

14 days of Pro, no credit card. After it lapses the free tier stays free.

What the Intellrise free tier does not do

For symmetry, the limits on the Intellrise side, so you are not surprised after signing up.

  • You must bring your own AI provider key. There is no platform key fallback on any tier, including paid ones. Without a key, the product cannot answer anything.
  • Bring-your-own-key is not free. You pay your provider for tokens. It is charged at their list price with no markup from Intellrise and it is predictable and linear, but it is not zero, and at very low volume a vendor's included quota can genuinely be cheaper.
  • One data source on Free, and three dashboards — and those three cannot be rearranged. Dashboard drag and resize, changing a chart's type or colours, and hand-editing the SQL behind a chart are all Pro. On the free tier a dashboard is what the product composed, not something you lay out.
  • No share links and no email delivery on Free. You can export every format, but distributing it is outside the product.
  • Unlimited data sources — the count never enters the price — plus file upload, dashboard customisation, share links, email delivery and the AI semantic layer are on Intellrise Pro, $29/mo, with a lower effective rate if you pay annually.
  • No file upload on Free, no notebooks at any tier, no .sav support, no Slack agent, and no public API.
  • The Team plan is not shipped yet — it is listed as coming, not available.

Those are the limits of the free plan. The 14 days of Pro that come first are the paid tier, not this one — and there is no card to cancel when they lapse.

Try Pro for 14 days, no card

14 days of Pro, no credit card. After it lapses the free tier stays free.

The one test worth running before you trust either of them

Neither this page nor any comparison page — ours included — can tell you the thing that actually decides this: whether the tool reads your particular schema correctly. The failure that costs you is not a missing feature. It is a column whose meaning is not in its name — a status integer where 3 means refunded rather than complete — being read the obvious way, and quietly producing a number you then send to somebody.

So run that test before you run any other. On whichever free tier fits where your data lives, connect or upload, ask one question that depends on your most misleading column, and check the answer against a number you already know is right. The Intellrise answer to that risk is not a claim, it is that the test is cheap: on the Intellrise free tier it costs one database connection and about twenty minutes. We are not going to tell you we pass it on your schema, because we have not seen your schema — but if Intellrise gets that column wrong, you have found out for free, on a number you could already check, rather than after you had sent it to your CEO.

Frequently asked questions

Is Julius AI free?

There is a free plan at $0. What is genuinely hard to answer is how much of it you get, because Julius publishes more than one figure. On 28 August 2026 its billing documentation gives two figures on one page: the credits table says "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily credits" and the prose under it "The Free plan's 25 welcome bonus credits are a one-time grant and don't renew", while the FAQ lower down says free users "receive a one-time grant of 100 credits when they sign up". The pricing page's comparison table says only "Free daily credits", with no number at all. On 3 August that table row read "100 (one-time)" instead, so the number has moved as well as being disputed. What every version agrees on is the shape: the free allowance is small, and continuing past it means a paid plan. Read from julius.ai on 3, 13 and 28 August 2026.

How many free credits does Julius give you, and do they renew?

Julius's own pages give two answers, so the honest reply is that you should count your own. Its credits documentation says free users "receive a one-time grant of 100 credits when they sign up; these credits don't renew", while the credits table on that same page read "25 welcome bonus + 25 daily credits" on 13 August 2026. Whichever you are granted, they do not roll over — asked directly whether unused credits roll over, Julius answers "No. Unused credits expire at the end of your billing cycle and don't carry over." And they cannot be extended by purchase: "At the moment, purchasing additional credits or topping up your balance is not supported." So the free plan has one budget with no refill mechanism of any kind.

How many questions do the free credits get you?

Julius does not publish a per-action credit price, and says so explicitly — its billing FAQ answers that there is no single answer because the cost depends on the complexity of the message and which tools it invokes. A quick question costs far less than a multi-step analysis that pulls data, runs code and produces a deliverable. Julius names model choice as one of the biggest drivers, with its faster in-house models consuming credits far more slowly than frontier ones. The only way to know your own rate is to watch the Usage page as you spend.

Can you connect a database on the Julius free plan?

No. On the pricing page's comparison table, the Data connectors row shows "Google Drive, OneDrive, Sharepoint" for the Free column, while Plus, Pro and Business add Snowflake, BigQuery and Postgres. So the free plan reads files from cloud storage, not live databases. Julius's own connector documentation lists PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Supabase and Vertica but does not state a plan requirement on those pages — the pricing table is the only Julius source that addresses the gating, so that is what we are citing. Read 3 August 2026 and re-read 28 August 2026, unchanged.

Does Julius AI have a free trial of its paid plans?

Not one that it advertises on its pricing page. We searched the rendered page and the underlying data payload on 3 August 2026 and again on 28 August 2026: the strings "trial", "free trial" and "credit card" return zero occurrences both times. The free plan itself is the evaluation path. For comparison, Intellrise offers a 14-day Pro trial with no card, and the account drops to the free tier afterwards rather than expiring.

What happens to your files on the Julius free plan?

They are deleted after an hour of inactivity. Julius's file documentation states that for free-tier users, files "are retained for up to 1 hour of inactivity, after which all uploaded and AI-generated files are deleted", while paid users keep files for up to 7 days of inactivity. Separately, the docs note that all containers, free and paid, spin down after an hour of inactivity. In practice this means the free plan supports a single working session rather than an analysis you return to.

Which AI models can you use on the Julius free plan?

One model, and the two Julius pages now agree on it. The model-selector documentation marks "Julius 1.2 Lite" as available on "All plans" and marks every other model — GPT-5.6 Sol, the Claude models, Grok and Kimi — as "Paid plans" or higher. The pricing page's comparison table matches: the Free column reads "Julius Lite models", Plus reads "Julius models, GPT-5.6, Claude Sonnet 5", and Pro and above read "All models, including Claude Fable 5". Both read 28 August 2026. We had a disagreement recorded here from 3 August, when the pricing table showed the Free column with the same model list as Plus; Julius has since fixed that, and we would rather say so than leave the old reading up. The docs page carries a caveat that plan availability can change and to check workspace settings, which is the safest advice we can pass on.

Does Julius still have a monthly message limit?

No, and this is the most common piece of stale information about Julius. Its documentation says plainly: "Instead of counting messages, Julius now measures usage in credits." Any comparison quoting a fixed number of messages per month on a Julius plan is describing a retired model. Julius's own site took a while to catch up, and we are updating this rather than leaving the old jab standing: on 3 August 2026 its service-description page was still describing Plus as providing "250 messages" and Pro as offering "unlimited messages", alongside a "Team plan at $50 per month per seat" that had already left the pricing page. When we re-read that page on 28 August 2026 it had been rewritten — the words message, messages and credits now return zero matches on it — so if you find a message count quoted anywhere about Julius today, it did not come from Julius.

Is there a free plan that connects to a live database?

Yes, and it is the main reason this comparison is worth reading rather than just checking Julius's pricing page. Julius gates live database connectors at Plus, $20/mo; the Intellrise free tier connects one live database at $0 — PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks or Redshift, with Google Sheets on top and not counted against the one. The trade is that Intellrise ships no platform AI key: you create a key with a provider such as Google, Anthropic or OpenAI, paste it in, and pay that provider for tokens directly at their price. If your data sits in a database and your budget is zero, that is usually the better trade. If your data is a spreadsheet on your laptop, it is the worse one, because a free Intellrise account cannot open an uploaded file at all — file upload is a Pro feature.

What does the Intellrise 14-day Pro trial include, and what happens after it?

A new account starts on Pro for 14 days with no card, so it includes the things the free tier does not: unlimited data sources instead of one, file upload, share links, email delivery of reports, and the AI semantic layer that learns what your columns mean and remembers it across sessions. When the 14 days lapse the account falls back to the permanently free tier rather than expiring or charging you, so there is nothing to cancel — which also means the honest way to use the trial is to spend it on the thing you cannot test for free, not on the thing you can.

What is the catch with a bring-your-own-key free tier?

That you have to bring a key. With Intellrise there is no credit meter and no per-question markup on any plan, so the free tier is not rationed the way a platform-key free tier has to be — but you must create an account with an AI provider and paste in a key before the product can answer anything, because there is no platform key fallback on any tier. You then pay that provider directly for tokens at list price. It is predictable and you control the model, but it is a slower start than signing up somewhere that includes the model, and at very low volume an included quota can cost you less.

This is a canonical repost. The original lives at https://intellrise.com/guides/julius-ai-free/ and is the copy we keep updated — if a figure here has moved, the original is the one that will say so.

title: 99.7% Rejected in 84ms: Why I Stopped Making the Generator Smarter
description:
I wrote a puzzle generator whose acceptance rate is 0.26%. It throws away 99.7% of everything it produces, and that is the design working as intended, not failing. Generating five valid puzzles takes 1,947 attempts and 84 milliseconds.

The point is not the puzzles. The point is that the generator makes no correctness guarantee at all, and a verifier makes every one of them. Once you split those two responsibilities, "make the generator smarter" stops being the obvious optimisation — and that is exactly the position you are in when the generator is an LLM.

The loop

verigen is a Go CLI that produces cryptarithmetic puzzles — alphametics, the SEND + MORE = MONEY genre, where each letter stands for a distinct digit and the sum has to hold. The known answer to that one is 9567 + 1085 = 10652.

There is one rule, and everything else follows from it:

The generator guarantees nothing. Every guarantee lives in the verifier.

The generator throws plausible-looking letter combinations at the wall. The verifier does an exhaustive search and confirms two things: that a solution exists, and that it is unique. Anything that fails either check is discarded and the loop asks for another candidate.

The loop itself knows nothing about cryptarithmetic. Implement a Domain interface and any other puzzle rides the same loop.

What the log actually says

Five puzzles, seed 7:

── Puzzle 2  [hard]
   HAIKU + BONSAI = KOKORO
   Answer: 96542 + 378165 = 474707
   (attempts before this seed landed: 624)

=== generate/verify loop [alphametic] ===
seed=7  output=5 puzzles  total attempts=1947  elapsed=84ms
acceptance rate = 0.2568%  (average 389 generations per puzzle)
--- rejection reasons ---
  no unique solution                  770  (39.55%)
  no solution                         695  (35.70%)
  more than 10 distinct letters       477  (24.50%)
  ok                                    5  ( 0.26%)

Nearly 40% of candidates have more than one valid solution. Another 36% have none. A quarter cannot possibly have one and are rejected before the search starts. Five survive.

Filtering by difficulty makes it worse: asking for easy puzzles drops the acceptance rate to 0.03%, about 3,200 generations each. It still finishes instantly.

I never tried to raise that number. Making the generator cleverer costs my time; making the verifier run 1,947 times costs 84ms. When generation is cheap, you can afford to be stupid on that side and pay for it in verification. The log is what makes that trade-off intuitive rather than theoretical — I did not really believe it until I saw 99.7% of the work land in the discard pile without the wall-clock time moving.

What the verifier has to guarantee

The loop is only worth as much as the assertions the verifier can actually make. For alphametics, that is:

Guarantee How
A solution exists Exhaustive search, column by column, carrying digits
The solution is unique Keep searching after the first hit; reject if a second exists
More than 10 distinct letters means no solution Pigeonhole. Rejected before the search runs
No leading zero Constrain the first letter of every multi-character word

Three design decisions made that table hold up.

I tested the verifier first. If the verifier is wrong, every guarantee downstream is a lie, and nothing in the output looks wrong. So the first tests were puzzles with published answers — SEND + MORE = MONEY → 9567 + 1085 = 10652, CROSS + ROADS = DANGER → 96233 + 62513 = 158746 — plus explicit cases for "no solution", "not unique", and the 11-letter rejection. The generator's tests came later. A broken generator lowers the acceptance rate; a broken verifier invalidates everything.

Pre-filtering only encodes facts, never heuristics. More than ten distinct letters cannot map to ten digits, so no solution exists — pigeonhole, not a guess. That check alone accounts for 24.5% of rejections and removes the most expensive searches before they begin. Note where the optimisation went: not into a smarter generator, but into the verifier's front door, rejecting hopeless candidates fast.

Difficulty is labelled a proxy, out loud. The difficulty score counts branch points during the search. That correlates with how much trial and error a human needs, probably — but I have not measured it against actual people, so the code and the docs both call it a proxy. Separating what you can assert from what you merely believe is not a nicety here. It is the discipline that keeps the word "verified" meaningful everywhere else.

Where this already is, and where it isn't

Swap the random generator for an LLM and the diagram is unchanged. That substitution is not a new idea in 2026 — in the major application areas it is already standard practice.

Code generation. Formalised as loop engineering: hooks and agent harnesses that refuse to let a run finish until tests, types and lint pass. Cognition's 2025 annual review put the merge rate of Devin-generated PRs at 67%, up from 34% the year before — while noting that roughly a third of those PRs still need substantial rework. Passing the verifier is the floor, not the goal.

SQL generation. Snowflake's Cortex Analyst moved automatic optimisation of verified queries into preview in December 2025. Vanna AI ships self-correction from dry-run errors as a standard feature. EXPLAIN, schema matching, and retry-on-execution-error are table stakes for text-to-SQL products.

Structured output. This one has gone past verification entirely: XGrammar constrains decoding so schema-violating tokens are never emitted, and it is now a standard backend in vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT. OpenAI's Structured Outputs works the same way. "Parse the JSON, catch the error, retry" is close to obsolete.

Proofs. The most spectacular case, and the most instructive, because this is where the pattern was tested against its own alternative.

AlphaProof, paired with AlphaGeometry 2, scored 28/42 at the 2024 IMO — silver-medal level, one point under the gold threshold. The mechanism is continuous with verigen: generate candidate proofs, run them through Lean 4 as a mechanical verifier, repeat until one passes, at enormous scale. DeepSeek-Prover-V2 is the same shape. What exhaustive search does for "this puzzle has exactly one solution", Lean does for "this theorem holds".

Then the following year, the verifier came out. Gemini Deep Think took gold at the 2025 IMO — 35/42, five of six problems — reasoning end-to-end in natural language, inside the human time limit, with no formal proof assistant anywhere in the loop, at roughly two orders of magnitude better inference efficiency than the 2024 approach. On the face of it that is a counterexample to everything I have argued.

Look at what each one was solving. An olympiad problem is an exam question: a solution is known to exist, the search space is bounded by the syllabus, and a human grader decides at the end. Deep Think did not need a mechanical verifier because a mechanical verifier was never the binding constraint there. Now compare AlphaProof Nexus, which in May 2026 reported solving 9 of 353 open Erdős problems and 44 of 492 open OEIS conjectures (arXiv:2605.22763) — including two open for 56 years. Nobody can grade that output. There is no answer key, and no human referee who can check the volume of candidates the system produces. Lean is not decoration in that setting; it is the only thing standing between "solved" and "claimed".

So the split is not verifier versus no verifier. It is whether anything else can decide the question. Where a competent grader exists, a strict verifier is an optimisation you may be able to skip. Where none exists, it is the entire basis on which you are allowed to use the word "solved".

The common precondition is that the verifier can decide the question mechanically. Where it cannot — is this prose any good? — the whole design has nothing to offer.

What is still open is the design of the verifiers themselves.

Round-trip verification. Transform the output back and check that it matches the input. Schema validation is everywhere; round-trip verification of semantic equivalence is not, and ETL and code migration between languages or frameworks are where it would pay.

A uniqueness-equivalent guarantee. My verifier does not stop at "a solution exists"; it asserts the solution is unique. The LLM equivalent is not stopping at "the code runs" but checking that behaviour is uniquely determined by the spec — property-based testing that finds no counterexample gets close.

A quality filter. verigen cannot reject a puzzle that is solvable but boring, and nothing in the LLM stack reliably rejects code that passes its tests but is badly designed. The metric itself is the unsolved part.

When this works

Three conditions, in order of how often they are the one that breaks:

The verifier must be strict — and honest about its limits. A verifier that appears to guarantee something it does not makes the entire loop a lie. Assert nothing you cannot assert. Labelling my difficulty score a proxy is the small version of this; treating "the tests pass" as "the code is correct" is the expensive version.

Generation must be cheap. 1,947 attempts in 84ms is why a 0.26% acceptance rate is survivable. An LLM call is hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, so the same acceptance rate would be absurd. With an expensive generator you have to tune both sides: prompts that raise the hit rate and a verifier strict enough to be worth the round trip.

Verification must not cost more than generation. Exhaustive search is expensive in principle and still fits inside those 84ms. Test suites and type checks do not always fit so comfortably. If verifying costs more than generating, the loop does not close.

What I'd build next

Classic puzzles were a deliberately easy setting: a domain where a verifier can make total guarantees by brute force, so I could think about verifier design without the verifier itself being the hard part. The loop is standard practice now. The interesting question has moved to what, exactly, your verifier is willing to assert.

Next on the list: a quality filter, since right now I only guarantee that a puzzle is solvable and nothing about whether it is worth solving; more domains (polyomino tiling is done, knots and definite integrals are candidates); and checking that difficulty proxy against actual human solvers, so I can stop calling it a proxy.

The repository: https://github.com/hidetzu/verigen

title: Returning RFC 9457 Problem Details from Go Validation Errors
description:
How to turn struct-tag validation failures into a standard "application/problem+json" response — the RFC 9457 format — with one method call, no hand-rolled error envelope.

Most Go APIs invent their own validation error shape. One team returns {"errors": [...]}, another {"field_errors": {...}}, a third just a flat {"error": "message"} and hopes the client parses it. Every one of those is a private contract the client has to learn from your docs, because there's no shared shape for "here's what's wrong with your request."

RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs — is the IETF standard that fixes this: a application/problem+json body with type, title, status, and room for problem-specific extensions. Checker now builds one of these directly from a failed struct validation, via CheckErrors.ProblemDetails().

The shape

RFC 9457 defines four base members — type, title, status, detail, instance — and lets a specific problem type add its own. For validation errors, RFC 9457 §3.1 sketches exactly this extension: an invalid-params array listing which fields failed and why. That's what Checker produces.

From a failed struct to a problem+json body

Take a struct with a missing required field:

type Person struct {
    Name string `checkers:"required"`
}

person := &Person{}

errs, ok := checker.CheckStruct(person)
if !ok {
    data, _ := json.Marshal(errs.ProblemDetails())
    fmt.Println(string(data))
}

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Your request parameters failed validation.",
  "status": 400,
  "invalid-params": [
    { "name": "Name", "reason": "Required value is missing.", "code": "REQUIRED" }
  ]
}

One method call — errs.ProblemDetails() — turns the same CheckErrors you'd otherwise call .JSON() on into a *ProblemDetails value, ready to marshal. type defaults to "about:blank" (RFC 9457's own default for "no more specific problem type registered"), status defaults to 400, and each invalid-params entry carries the field name, a localized human-readable reason, and the machine-readable code — the same code you'd branch on client-side with the plain .JSON() output.

Wiring it into a handler

The one thing RFC 9457 requires that a plain JSON body doesn't is the content type:

func signupHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var req SignupRequest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "invalid JSON", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    errs, valid := checker.CheckStruct(&req)
    if !valid {
        pd := errs.ProblemDetails()

        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/problem+json")
        w.WriteHeader(pd.Status)
        json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(pd)
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
}

pd.Status drives both the header and the body, so they can't drift out of sync.

Overriding the defaults

Type, Title, and Status are plain exported fields on the returned *ProblemDetails — RFC 9457 deliberately leaves them to the API producer, so Checker fills in reasonable defaults and gets out of your way. Set them before marshaling if you want a registered problem type or a different status code:

pd := errs.ProblemDetails()
pd.Type = "https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error"
pd.Title = "Signup request failed validation"
pd.Status = http.StatusUnprocessableEntity // 422 instead of 400

Nothing else about the call changes — invalid-params is still built from the same CheckErrors map.

Localized problem details

Since ProblemDetails() is just ProblemDetailsWithLocale(DefaultLocale) under the hood, a localized variant is one argument away — same 23 locales that back JSONWithLocale:

pd := errs.ProblemDetailsWithLocale(locales.DeDE)

The reason strings come back in German; type, status, and code are untouched, since those aren't meant for display.

Why bother with a standard shape

A hand-rolled error envelope works fine until you have more than one API, or a client library trying to handle errors generically, or an API gateway that wants to do something useful with 4xx bodies without special-casing your service. application/problem+json is already understood by tooling in several ecosystems — Spring, ASP.NET Core, and various API gateways emit or consume it natively — so producing it from Go costs you nothing extra (it's the same validation you were already running) and buys you a body shape other tools don't have to be taught.

Try it 

go get github.com/cinar/checker/v2

import checker "github.com/cinar/checker/v2"

ProblemDetails() and ProblemDetailsWithLocale() sit right next to JSON() and JSONWithLocale() on CheckErrors — pick whichever body shape your API needs, from the same validation call. Full details in the README.

title: Testing WhatsApp Activity Pipelines: A Contract-First Approach with Fixtures
description:
When building data pipelines that process external signals—like checking WhatsApp account activity—the biggest bottleneck isn't the API itself; it's the fragility of your local parsing logic. If your downstream system expects a specific schema from a CSV export, a minor change in the upstream data format can break your entire ingestion pipeline.

To build a robust integration, you should treat the WhatsApp Activity Checker as a contract. By using local test fixtures, you can validate your normalization and mapping logic without hitting the production API repeatedly.

The Asynchronous Challenge

The WhatsApp Activity Checker uses an asynchronous batch workflow. You submit a file to POST /v1/tasks, poll POST /v1/gettasks for status, and eventually download a result file from the result_url once the status is exported.

Because this process involves file I/O and network latency, writing tests that rely on live calls is slow and prone to failure. Instead, decouple your logic into two layers:

  1. The Client Layer: Handles the X-API-Key authentication and polling logic.
  2. The Processor Layer: Handles the CSV parsing and field mapping.

Step 1: Define Your Contract Fixtures

Create a fixtures/ directory in your project. This allows you to simulate the exported state of a task. Create a mock_results.csv file that mirrors the expected output format:

number,activated,activetime,activedays,business
+14155552671,yes,2023-10-01,15,no
+442071838750,yes,2023-09-28,42,yes

Step 2: Implement the Processor Unit Test

Your unit tests should focus on how your application maps these fields. By using the fixture file, you ensure your code handles the activetime and business fields correctly, even if the API structure evolves.

# Example: Testing the mapper logic
def test_csv_parser_mapping():
 # Load your fixture
 data = load_csv_fixture("fixtures/mock_results.csv")

 # Validate mapping logic
 result = map_to_internal_schema(data[0])

 assert result["is_active"] == True
 assert result["is_business"] == False

Step 3: Integration Boundaries

When you move from local testing to the real v1/tasks endpoint, ensure your integration layer is resilient to the asynchronous nature of the service.

  • Poll, don't guess: Only initiate your download logic when the status returned by v1/gettasks is strictly exported.
  • Normalize inputs: Always ensure your input file contains numbers in E.164 format before sending them to the file field in your POST request.
  • Handle failures: The exported file will contain both successful and failed rows. Ensure your parser checks the failure count returned in the status response to log discrepancies early.

Conclusion

By moving your testing focus to local fixtures, you isolate your business logic from the network-heavy polling workflow. This approach allows you to iterate on your data pipeline safely, ensuring that when you do trigger a production task, your system is already prepared to handle the results correctly. For the latest details on endpoints and status codes, always refer to the official documentation.
